summary: Intro scoping for a short pilot to validate TTFT vs TPOT SLOs across Zenith's chat workloads. Agreed to a 3-scenario benchmark (short-turn chat, long-context generation, high-concurrency throughput). Defined preliminary p95/p99 targets and a measurement plan including warmup, sample sizes, and instrumentation. Action items and next steps assigned.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood), Maya (Zenith ML Lead), Samir (Zenith SRE), Liam (Zenith PM), Nora (Zenith Security)

[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick round robin, then we'll jump into the SLOs and the benchmark plan.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Hi all, Maya here. we're mostly focused on chat agent latency and cost, want to scope a pilot to see tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated.
[00:27] Priya Nair: Awesome. quick clarifier: are you prioritizing time to first token, or sustained token throughput? or both?
[00:35] Liam O'Neal: Both, ideally. TTFT because UX matters for short interactions, TPOT for long generative flows where cost matters.
[00:44] Samir Patel: Also need to see how caching helps — KV cache hit rates will change effective TPOT. we have a lot of repeated system prompts.
[00:55] Alex Mercer: Good. for alignment today we propose three scenarios: 1) short-turn chat (<=128 tokens), 2) long-context generation (500-2k tokens), 3) sustained load (peak concurrency) to understand throughput.
[01:07] Jordan Lee: We'll capture both TTFT (time from request accepted to first token) and TPOT (avg time per token after first) plus p50/p95/p99.
[01:16] Nora Diaz: On security side we need audit logs, KMS integration, and a clear data residency note. we'll validate once you share the compliance pack.
[01:25] Maya Chen: timeline: want pilot results within three weeks if possible.
[01:29] Priya Nair: That is doable. quick straw targets to discuss: for short-turn chat, TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 700ms. TPOT p95 <= 45ms/token, p99 <= 90ms/token for mid-size model - these are starting points, can be tuned per model family.
[01:46] Maya Chen: those numbers seem aggressive but ok as starting. can you explain measurement methodology?
[01:51] Priya Nair: Sure. we'll run synthetic and real prompt sampling. methodology: 1) warm-up window (10-15min) to populate KV cache and JIT kernels; 2) steady state measurement window (recommended 10 minutes per scenario) capturing at least 1k requests per scenario; 3) collect p50/p95/p99 TTFT and token latency, batch distribution, GPU util, and percent of requests served from cache.
[02:21] Samir Patel: For throughput tests, what's your approach to batching? we don't want to introduce high tail latency by trying to maximize tokens per batch.
[02:28] Priya Nair: We'll test multiple batching profiles: conservative (max batch 8), balanced (16), and aggressive (32+). Redwood runtime supports continuous batching; we'll log batch sizes and correlate with latency percentiles.
[02:42] Alex Mercer: Also will simulate client-side concurrency and a service-side autoscaling profile so we measure both raw throughput and how infra scales.
[02:51] Maya Chen: Can you quantify TPOT targets for long-context flows?
[02:55] Priya Nair: For long-context we'll look at amortized TPOT — target p95 of ~60ms/token and p99 <= 120ms/token for 1k token outputs on a quantized M model. again varies by model/quantization/hardware.
[03:12] Liam O'Neal: We have a budget constraint: around X dollars per million tokens; if cost exceeds we'd need to consider quant or smaller model.
[03:19] Alex Mercer: We'll include cost per 1k tokens estimate in the report per model variant and quantization option.
[03:25] [Crosstalk] Samir Patel: what's the difference we're measuring between TTFT and cold-start?
[03:30] Priya Nair: Good point — we'll measure cold TTFT (after instance spin or after KV flush) and warm TTFT (after a sustained warm window). Cold is expected to be higher; acceptance criteria typically focus on warm p95/p99 but we'll show both.
[03:44] Maya Chen: For acceptance criteria, do you require both p95 and p99 to pass? or is it weighted?
[03:49] Alex Mercer: We recommend passing p95 for primary acceptance and p99 must not exceed a hard ceiling; team agreed earlier on p95 thresholds as primary, p99 as guardrails.
[03:58] Priya Nair: Measurement details: sampling size of at least 1,000 successful responses per scenario, statistical outlier removal for infra noise (we'll annotate events like autoscaler cold windows), collect system metrics at 1s granularity.
[04:13] Jordan Lee: We'll instrument with Prometheus metrics and send a CSV of raw latencies + aggregated percentiles. also provide a notebook to reproduce plots.
[04:22] Maya Chen: How about test harness? we prefer something reproducible — can you share the repo?
[04:26] Alex Mercer: Yes, I'll share the benchmark harness link in the follow-ups — it's a lightweight runner that supports replaying prompt CSVs, variable concurrency, and collects token-level timestamps.
[04:39] Samir Patel: Networking: we'll need an allowlist for test IPs; for private deployment we'll schedule a VPC peering window.
[04:45] Alex Mercer: noted — Samir you'll get the access instructions.
[04:48] Nora Diaz: on compliance, we'll need SOC2 and encryption-at-rest details.
[04:52] Alex Mercer: We'll push the compliance pack and a 1-pager on encryption/KMS integration.
[04:58] Liam O'Neal: ok on sample prompt sets: we have three categories: transactional chat, knowledge retrieval, and long form creative. we'll upload them.
[05:07] Priya Nair: Good. measurement plan also includes: 1) cold-start TTFT sample (10 cold runs), 2) warm-run steady-state (1k runs), 3) sustained ramp to peak concurrency to observe dropping throughput or tail spikes.
[05:22] Maya Chen: Any recommended p99 tolerances when using dedicated GPUs? our internal SLA requires p99 under 1.2s for UX.
[05:31] Priya Nair: For dedicated, p99 typically improves — we should set model-specific ceilings. we'll run the dedicated baseline and share the per-model ceilings in the report; as a heuristic we suggested 700ms for short-turn p99.
[05:45] Alex Mercer: We'll also include a regression test set — a set of prompt-response pairs gold-checks to ensure quality doesn't degrade when we quantize or tune kernels.
[05:55] Maya Chen: what's the plan for analyzing tradeoffs in cost vs latency?
[05:59] Jordan Lee: We'll compute cost per successful request and cost per token for each model/quantization/batching config. deliverable will have a cost-latency frontier chart.
[06:08] Samir Patel: Instrumentation detail: we need token timestamps with microsecond-ish resolution? is that available?
[06:14] Priya Nair: We capture token emission timestamps on the runtime side; granularity depends on infra but we provide fine-grained timing sufficient to compute TPOT. in our harness we compute time to first token then avg token intervals.
[06:27] Liam O'Neal: For the pilot acceptance, propose: pass short-turn p95 and cost-per-1k within budget. if not both, then plan a follow-on optimization phase.
[06:36] Alex Mercer: That sounds reasonable — we'll draft a pilot charter with explicit pass/fail.
[06:40] Nora Diaz: Security question: where are logs stored and how long retained?
[06:44] Alex Mercer: Default retention is 30d, enterprise can extend. logs are stored in encrypted buckets with KMS. we'll include details.
[06:52] Maya Chen: Any thought on sampling strategies for percentile stability? we want p99 to be statistically meaningful.
[06:58] Priya Nair: For p99 stability we recommend 10k samples if you want high confidence; for pilot we aim for 1k per scenario and flag p99 confidence intervals. if p99 fluctuates we'll rerun longer windows.
[07:13] Samir Patel: How are you distinguishing infra noise like network glitches vs model runtime?
[07:18] Jordan Lee: We'll correlate client-side latencies with server-side metrics (GPU util, cuda context switches, batch sizes) and annotate known network events. also run control tests from the same VPC to minimize network variability.
[07:36] Maya Chen: Great. can you summarize the deliverables?
[07:40] Alex Mercer: Deliverables: 1) benchmark harness + runbook, 2) raw CSVs + aggregated percentiles and plots, 3) cost-latency tradeoff report per model variant, 4) pilot acceptance charter with pass/fail criteria, 5) compliance pack and security Qs answered.
[07:58] Priya Nair: We'll also provide a short notebook reproducing the p95/p99 computations and a notebook for the cost frontier.
[08:06] Liam O'Neal: timeline again? you said three weeks earlier for pilot results.
[08:10] Alex Mercer: Rough timeline: week 0 (this week) agreement and data transfer, week 1 bench runs and tuning, week 2 extended runs and analysis, week 3 deliverable and review. that's ~3 weeks.
[08:22] Maya Chen: ok we'll try to upload prompts and traffic hist by Monday.
[08:25] Samir Patel: I'll coordinate VPC peering windows after we get the run windows.
[08:30] Alex Mercer: Cool. any last questions?
[08:33] Nora Diaz: just confirm you'll share SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[08:36] Alex Mercer: Yes, will share.
[08:38] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Alex Mercer: Thanks — recap and next steps will be in the follow-up email.

Post-meeting notes (auto): we captured three benchmark scenarios, initial SLO targets (short-turn TTFT p95<=250ms, p99<=700ms; TPOT p95<=45ms/token, p99<=90ms/token), plan for warm vs cold measurement, batch profile exploration, cost-latency reporting, and security/compliance deliverables. next steps assigned as action items.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings of acronyms (TTFT sometimes appear as T-T-F-TT or TTF), 'TPOT' sometimes transcribed as T-plot; names occasionally garbled (Samir sometimes 'Sameer').
